$comment: The committed size of the code-scanning backlog, and the only thing that reads it is
the `Code scanning backlog` job in security.yml.
WHY A NUMBER AND NOT ZERO. `github/codeql-action/analyze` fails on nothing: it uploads
every alert the security-and-quality suite raises and reports success either way. So the
page has been accumulating findings that no gate has ever read, and demanding zero on the
first run would red every pull request over a backlog none of them created — the failure
mode the allocation gate exists to avoid, and the one that made the Semgrep job worthless
for months.
SO IT IS A RATCHET. The job fails when the open count exceeds `total`, which makes a new
alert a failure today. Lowering the number is the work; raising it is a decision that has
to be argued in the pull request that raises it, because nothing else here can move.
HOW TO RE-RECORD. Read the count the job prints, fix alerts until it drops, and set
`total` to what remains. Never set it to what the run reported without looking at the
difference: a count that rose because a query pack was updated is a different fact from
one that rose because somebody wrote a defect.
WHAT `total` COUNTS: alerts against code that ships. Two sets are excluded, both counted
and listed by the job so neither disappears. obj/generated, because fixing one means
changing a generator that emits the same shape on purpose and CodeQL cannot be told to
skip them — 1,988 of 2,234 when last measured. And tests/, because a finding there is in
code no deployment runs: the fixtures that trip cs/path-combine are string literals naming
files in the working tree, and holding a release to those teaches people to raise this
number, which is the one move that ends the gate.
WHY IT MOVED FROM 240 TO 144. Not because 96 alerts were fixed. 240 was measured over
authored code including tests/; this is the same measurement with tests/ taken out (102
of the 246 authored on dev at 0f9d769). The rule mix under it also changed substantially
between those two readings — cs/call-to-gc went from 9 to 0, cs/local-not-disposed from 18
to 4, cs/path-combine from 49 to 27, while cs/useless-upcast (24), cs/useless-cast-to-self
(14), cs/missed-using-statement (5) and cs/dispose-not-called-on-throw (4) appeared. Four
families arriving and two leaving is a query pack that moved, not code that rotted.
`bySeverity` is not enforced. It is here so a re-recording says which way the backlog
moved, rather than only that it did. It is null pending the first run under the shipped/
tests split, which prints the severity counts this should then record.
The ceiling binds on pushes to master, dev and release/** only, because a pull request
analysis is annotated rather than persisted and has no alerts to count. See the backlog job.
